description: Nigerians describe volunteering evidence nobody asked for - references, certificates, receipts - to forestall a doubt that has not yet been expressed. It is exhausting and it is rational.
energy_note: Proving yourself before anyone has doubted you.

aspect: Anger at the actual fraudsters, which has nowhere to go
description: The resentment among ordinary Nigerians towards the people who built the reputation is intense, and expressing it abroad reads as confirming the stereotype rather than distancing from it.
energy_note: Furious at them, and unable to say so without sounding like them.

aspect: Children inherit it without the context
description: Second-generation children are asked about the prince joke in a playground in a country their parents chose, with no framework for it and no memory of Nigeria at all.

aspect: It suppresses the very thing that would change it
description: Visibility - starting the company, taking the platform, publishing under your own name - is what would eventually replace the stereotype, and it is exactly what the stereotype makes costly.
energy_note: The cure is the thing it makes expensive.

description: His daughter is nine, born in Manchester, and asks at dinner what a Nigerian prince is, because a boy at school said it. He has about four seconds to decide how much of the last thirty years to explain to a nine-year-old.
energy_note: Four seconds to decide how much to tell her.
